claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC alloy.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
The limited plasticity of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is caused or aggravated by its high Mo content.
V has lower electronegativity than Mo.
Replacing approximately 15% of the Mo sublattice with V produces Nb20Zr20Ti20Hf20Mo17V3 in atomic-percent terms.
Partial substitution of Mo by V lowers the alloy's overall electronegativity mismatch.
The proposed V-substituted alloy retains a disordered, single-phase BCC structure.
Partial Mo-to-V substitution modifies the lattice distortion of the BCC matrix.
Lower electronegativity mismatch creates a softer bonding environment.
The softer bonding environment lowers barriers to dislocation motion.
Residual Mo and inherent lattice distortion preserve high yield strength after V substitution.
Partial Mo-to-V substitution increases room-temperature compressive strain to failure relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
The V-substituted alloy maintains room-temperature compressive yield strength near or above 1700 MPa.
The strength-plasticity benefit occurs within a narrow V-substitution range of roughly 10–15 at%.
Exceeding the proposed substitution range may destabilize the BCC phase or cause an undesirable reduction in yield strength.
Arc melting followed by inert-atmosphere homogenization can produce a uniform, single-phase disordered BCC alloy in the proposed compositional range.

contradictions.description: The notation NbZrTiHf(Mo0.85V0.15) replaces 15% of the Mo site and therefore gives only about 3 at% V overall, whereas the boundary describes the operative range as roughly 10–15 at% V overall.

The boundary anticipates possible phase instability above the narrow target range, but the falsification rule can reject the hypothesis if any V-substituted alloy in the tested x = 0–0.20 series loses the BCC phase, including deliberately out-of-range compositions.
